title: Check yourself: Orchestrators, evaluators, agents and the practice

questions.stem: A coding tool must change several files, but nobody can say in advance how many or which. Which pattern suits it?

options.text: Prompt chaining, with one fixed step for each file
options.says: Ruled out because chaining is ideal when the task "can be easily and cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks", and here the number of files is not known.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: a central model plans and delegates
options.says: The page says orchestrator-workers is "well-suited for complex tasks where you can't predict the subtasks needed", with coding as its example.

options.text: Routing, with one handler for each file extension
options.says: Ruled out because routing "works well for complex tasks where there are distinct categories that are better handled separately", which is a choice of one path and not a plan with a variable length.

options.text: Voting, with the same edit run several times for agreement
options.says: Ruled out because "Running the same task multiple times to get diverse outputs" is voting, which repeats one task and does not split a task.

questions.stem: A pipeline makes many calls, uses search and code execution, and runs for minutes while the user waits. What would make the article call it an agent?

options.text: Making its calls in parallel and not in sequence
options.says: Ruled out because "Sectioning splits the task into independent parts" and the page says "All of them are workflows", so parallel calls stay a workflow.

options.text: Using further tools such as a browser or a database
options.says: Ruled out because every pattern calls "an LLM enhanced with augmentations such as retrieval, tools, and memory", so tools do not mark an agent.

options.text: Running for hours and not minutes before it answers
options.says: Ruled out because the line is drawn by who decides, as in "dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage", and not by how long a run lasts.

options.text: Letting the LLM, not the program, choose each next step
options.says: The page says agents "dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage".

origin.section: The earlier patterns, side by side

questions.stem: A draft-and-review loop has no accepted draft after the allowed rounds. What does the practice's refine function return?

options.text: The last draft, since later revisions always improve on earlier ones
options.says: Ruled out because "a late revision can be worse", which is why the best draft wins.

options.text: The highest-scoring version so far, and on a tie the earlier one
options.says: The page says that after the maximum rounds "the best draft wins, not the last one", and the earliest wins a tie.

options.text: Nothing, because the loop keeps running until a draft passes
options.says: Ruled out because "The autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors", which is the cost of a loop with no exit.

options.text: An error, since failing to reach the threshold is a failure
options.says: Ruled out because agents and loops "include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control", so reaching the maximum is a planned end and not a failure.
